# Wood Stove Flue Sweep

## Overview

I sweep the flue once a year, in late summer, before the first fire of the season goes in. A year of burning leaves a lining of creosote on the inside of the pipe, a tar that starts as a brown stain and dries into something like varnish. Left alone it thickens, and thick creosote is what burns when a flue fire starts, at temperatures the pipe and the chimney breast were never built to take. A sweep takes me about two hours and costs nothing but the hire of a ladder, and it tells me the state of the whole system while I am up there. I pick a dry, still day: dry so the roof is safe to stand on, still so the soot drops straight down the flue instead of blowing about the loft. The ladder gets tied off at the gutter before I climb, and I take the rods, the brush and a roll of tape up in one trip. I do it myself rather than pay a sweep, partly for the money and partly because going up there myself means I see the state of the pot, the flashing and the cap while I am at it. The whole job is inside two hours including the test fire, and it is the cheapest hour of the year for peace of mind.

## Steps

I start by laying dust sheets. One over the hearth and out across the rug beyond it, one over the wood floor, with the edges turned up and tucked so any soot that lands stays on the sheet. I move the log basket, the tools and the fire gloves out of the room entirely. Then the ladder goes up at the gable, tied off at the gutter, with the feet on firm ground and the top resting on the wall, not the gutter itself. Once the ladder is set I take the rods up in their bag and lay them out on the roof beside the pot.

I sweep from the pot end downwards, pulling the brush down the flue in short strokes so the soot falls ahead of it and drops into the firebox. Working from the pot means I am not pushing soot into the room, and it keeps the brush free of the heavy deposits near the top where the pipe runs cold against the outside wall. The brush goes down the flue on the rods, a section at a time, until I feel it pass the register plate and hit the bottom of the run. Then I pull it up, add another rod, and go again. Two or three passes are usually enough if the flue has not been left too long.

Before I sweep, I tape a heavy bag round the stove opening. A bin bag with the mouth taped flat across the face of the stove, right round the door frame, catches the soot as it falls and stops the room filling with the fine dust that gets everywhere if you leave the firebox open. I cut a small slit in the bag when I am ready to drop the brush through, and I tape that shut again between passes. The stove door stays closed for the whole sweep, and the bag does the work.

The baffle plate has to come out first, and it has to go back exactly as it came out. On this stove it is a steel plate that sits above the firebricks on two ledges, and it lifts forward and drops down once I tilt the front edge. I photograph it in place before I touch it, because on the first sweep I put it back the wrong way round and the stove smoked into the room until I worked out what I had done. Out it comes, and it goes on a sheet on the floor, top side up, with the firebricks left in place. The firebox gets a quick brush round while the plate is off and the bag is still taped over the opening.

With the plate out I can see up to the register plate, and that is where I look hardest. The register plate is the steel sheet that closes the bottom of the chimney and takes the flue collar, and it should be sealed to the brick with fire cement or rope, with no gaps at the corners. I check it with a torch and a mirror, following the seam right round. On the third sweep I found a gap about 5 mm wide at the back corner where the cement had cracked and fallen away, and I could feel cold air pulling down through it on a still evening. I raked out the old cement and packed new rope seal into the seam, then smoothed fire cement over it and let it set overnight. A gap there is a small flue fire waiting to happen, and it also lets the stove run cold and smoky.

The soot that has come down gets lifted out with the vacuum. I use a small ash vacuum with a fine filter, the sort sold for stove work, because a household vacuum will not survive the dust and the hot grit. The bag comes off the stove opening once the plates are back, and the vacuum goes round the firebox floor, the ledges and the bag itself before I fold it shut. I weigh the bag out of habit. A normal year gives me about two kg of soot and dust, and a year where I have burned wet wood gives more, closer to three kg, and comes down in heavy clumps rather than a fine powder.

The baffle plate then goes back, in the right way round, sitting level on its ledges. The firebricks get checked for cracks while I am in there, and I swap any that have split clean through. The door goes shut, the air control is left open, and I light a small test fire to prove the draw. It should catch quickly and burn bright with the flames going up the flue, and there should be no smoke curling out round the door or the top plate. If the test fire smoulders or spills into the room, something in the reassembly is wrong and I do not leave the stove until I have found it.

The brush size is the one part of the kit I would not guess at. My flue is a 125 mm liner, and the brush that does the job is a 150 mm one, 25 mm over the diameter of the flue. That 25 mm is enough to press the bristle tips against the whole wall of the liner and knock the creosote off, and not so much that the brush jams in the run or turns itself inside out on the way down. The first year I borrowed a 100 mm brush from a neighbour, because it looked about right, and it skimmed the middle of the flue and left a brown band of tar all the way round the wall. The next year I bought the 150 mm brush and the liner came up grey metal from top to bottom, and the sweep took a third of the time because the brush was actually doing the work instead of polishing the air. I keep the brush in a bag with the rods and mark the size on the handle so I never pick up the wrong one.

## Notes

A partial blockage behaves differently from a full one and it is worth knowing which you have. A partial blockage gives a lazy fire, smoke that hangs about the top plate and a stove that will not pull, while a full blockage puts smoke back into the room the moment the door opens. To tell them apart I open the door an inch on a cold stove and hold a lit taper near the top of the opening: a good draw pulls the flame in, a partial blockage leaves it standing, and a full one pushes it away. The chimney cap at the pot gets checked every sweep, since it can rust shut or fill with soot and stop the draw on its own. Bird nests are the common summer problem, and the first autumn fire usually shifts them, but if the draw is poor after a quiet summer I go up and look before I burn anything, because a nest plus a hot fire is how flues catch. Smoke spillage indoors is the signal to stop and check, never to burn harder. I keep a note of the sweep date taped inside the stove cupboard, and I check the flashing and the pot mortar while the ladder is up.

## Maintenance

The baffle plate and the firebricks are the two parts I look at every year when the flue is open. The baffle warps over time and a warped plate lets heat straight up the flue, so I check it sits flat on the ledges with no rock in it, and I replace it once the sag has gone past a few millimetres. Firebricks crack from the heat cycles and get replaced before they break through, since a broken brick exposes the steel body to the full heat of the fire and that is how a stove body fails. The door rope seal gets a look while I have the gloves out; it flattens with use and a flattened seal leaks air past the glass. I sweep in late summer, six weeks before the season starts, so there is time to order a part if the sweep turns anything up. I keep a spare firebrick and a length of rope on the shelf, because both fail at the worst time of year and a week without the stove in January is a cold week. The glass gets cleaned with a damp cloth and a dip of ash when the season opens, and the ash pan is emptied into a metal bucket every few days.
